opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, honestly, the first thing that strikes you is just how messy it is, and I mean that in the best possible way. When we started pulling Open X-Embodiment together, we were collecting data from dozens of labs around the world, and every lab had made its own choices. You've got single-arm manipulators like Frankas, xArms, UR5s, and Kinovas. You've got mobile manipulators like the Everyday Robots platform we used at Google. There are bimanual setups and even some quadrupeds in there. The camera placements are different, the control frequencies are different, the action spaces are different. Some people are doing end-effector control, some are doing joint control. The grippers vary too, and so do the scenes, from kitchens to tabletops to toy setups.

The conventional wisdom in robotics for a long time was that this heterogeneity is a bug. The thinking was that you collect data on your robot, in your lab, for your task, and that data is basically useless to anyone else. Each lab was its own little island.

What surprised a lot of us, and I think this was the real headline, is that when you train one big model across all of that diversity, you get positive transfer. The RT-1-X and RT-2-X models trained on the mixture often outperformed the specialist models that each lab had trained on its own data, sometimes by a meaningful margin, especially for the smaller datasets. And with RT-2-X, we saw emergent skills show up on our robot that only existed in the data from other robots. The model could do spatial reasoning and understand prepositions in ways it couldn't from our data alone.

So my takeaway is that the diversity in embodiments is starting to look less like noise and more like a feature. It's a lot like what we saw in language and vision. When you mix a bunch of different sources, the model learns something more general about the underlying structure. In robotics, that structure is something like what it means to physically interact with objects in the world, independent of what particular arm you happen to be.

That said, I want to be honest that we're still really early. The embodiments are diverse, but the dataset is still heavily skewed toward tabletop pick-and-place with parallel-jaw grippers. We don't have much dexterous hand data, much long-horizon mobile manipulation, or much contact-rich stuff. So a big open question for me is how far this scales. If we keep adding wildly different bodies, do we keep getting positive transfer, or do we hit a point where the embodiments are too different and they start interfering with each other? My intuition, given everything we've seen with scaling in other domains, is that bigger models will absorb that diversity better. That's a large part of why I'm optimistic about the whole cross-embodiment direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes diverse embodiments, including single-arm and mobile manipulators, bimanual setups, and quadrupeds, and contrasts that diversity with the conventional view that data collected for one robot, lab, and task was not useful elsewhere.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most is just how different these robots are from each other. When we pulled together Open X-Embodiment, we ended up with something like twenty-two distinct robot types from over thirty labs, and that wasn't a curated spread. It was just what people happened to have in their buildings. So you've got Franka arms, you've got WidowX, xArms, Google's EDR robots, UR5s, a few bimanual setups, even some mobile manipulators. Different numbers of joints, different grippers, different camera placements, different control frequencies, totally different action spaces in some cases.

And the honest expectation going in, at least for a lot of us, was that this heterogeneity would be a problem. The intuition from classic robot learning is that you want your training distribution to match your test robot as tightly as possible. Different embodiment felt like it should be noise at best and actively harmful at worst.

What actually struck me was that it wasn't. When we trained RT-1-X and RT-2-X on the combined mix, the models did better on the individual labs' robots than models trained only on that lab's own data. In some cases a lot better, like fifty percent improvement on average in the emergent skills evaluations. So the diversity turned out to be the asset, not the liability. The model was picking up something shared across embodiments: how to parse a scene, where objects are, what "move toward the cup" means in roughly image-space terms, and then mapping that onto whatever body it happened to be driving.

The other thing that strikes me is how much it rhymes with what happened in language and vision. Nobody would think you should train a language model on only one author's writing because the test distribution is that author. The diversity is where the generalization comes from. Robotics just hadn't had the scale to see that effect before, partly because no single lab could collect across that many embodiments alone. The dataset only exists because a bunch of groups were willing to pool what they had, and I think that collaborative aspect ends up being as important as the technical result.

r001.rationale: The response describes about twenty-two robot types with different joints, grippers, and other embodiment features, and says the variety was not curated. It also notes the expectation that training data should closely match the test robot.

astra-6.text:
What’s striking is that it’s not just a bunch of different robots that look slightly different. You have single arms, two-arm systems, different grippers, different camera setups. And each of those changes what the robot observes and how it acts in the world.

But underneath that, there’s a lot of shared structure. Picking up an object still involves recognizing it, understanding where it is, and figuring out how to approach it. So the exciting question is whether training on all of those embodiments lets a model learn something more general about manipulation—and whether experience from one robot can actually help another robot. That’s what makes the diversity so interesting: it becomes a potential source of better learning.

r001.rationale: The response describes varied embodiments—single-arm and two-arm systems, grippers, and camera setups—but does not state that this diversity contrasts with restrictive dataset selection assumptions.

sol-6.1.text: What’s striking is how different these robots are. You have different arm configurations, different grippers, different camera placements, and different ways of representing actions. So this isn’t just collecting more demonstrations on essentially the same robot. It raises a really interesting question: how much of what a robot learns is specific to its body, and how much is a more general understanding of a task? Picking something up has common structure across embodiments, even if the precise movements are different. That’s what makes pooling these datasets exciting—the possibility that experience from one robot can help another robot learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes varied arm configurations and grippers, communicating embodiment diversity, but does not state that this diversity exists despite restrictive dataset selection assumptions.
